newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada unemployment rate rises ahead of election.
newsitem.headline: Canada unemployment rate rises ahead of election.

text.p: Canada's unemployment rate jumped to 9.6 percent in April, Statistics Canada said on Friday in its last jobless report before the June 2 federal election.
Economists had expected the rate to remain unchanged at 9.3 percent, but it rose in most of the country's 10 provinces.
The main reason for the rise was that 79,000 people joined the work force, swamping the estimated 33,000 jobs that were added, mostly in self-employment. Total employment was 13.83 million.
The ruling Liberals' opponents were certain to jump on the unemployment rate as proof current policies were not working, while the Liberals took comfort from the number of new jobs.
"There is job creation, 33,000 more jobs, which is very positive," Prime Minister Jean Chretien's spokesman, Patrick Parisot, told Reuters. "The climate of the economy is getting better."
For most of Chretien's 3-1/2 years in office, the unemployment rate has been stubbornly stuck between 9 percent and 10 percent.
Chretien has said governments do not create jobs, but his right-wing opponents have said it would help if he cut taxes, especially on payrolls.
"I would say (the report) was neutral to positive. Employment has been way behind the rest of the economy," said Randall Powley, senior economist at brokerage ScotiaMcLeod Inc.

Lehman Brothers economist Michael Gregory said it was a mixed bag, but added: "On balance, this is a good report. It shows that the Canadian economy may be finally moving in a self-propogating mode, where internal job growth fuels consumption, which then keeps the process going."
Calculating the rate is an imprecise science.

Statistics Canada said that because it takes only a sample of Canadian employment, its employment number should have a margin of error of 62,000 jobs 95 percent of the time, or 32,000 jobs 67 percent of the time.
